problems: Nazianzen's learning line is cut off before its point. The part shown only praises 'education'. The words that matter, the outside learning 'which many Christians ill-judgingly abhor', come after the '…', so the line does not show him agreeing about learning from people outside the faith.

Nazianzen's church line needs a footnote to work. 'New Pharisee', 'the sentiments of Novatus' and 'dischargest' mean nothing to a choir alto. The part that lands is the last two questions ('Will you not give any place to weeping? Will you shed no tear?'). Show those with one plain lead-in.
Basil's church line stops at 'involves the …', so his point never arrives: one open sin drags the whole church in.

The kindred spirit was chosen on only five shared statements, because she answered Not sure to six. It happens to feel right, but the lead over Isaac (0.95 vs 0.81) rests mostly on the one church statement.

Missed delight: Nazianzen and Basil were best friends from their student days in Athens, and nothing says so. It gets worse: Nazianzen's laugh line praises Basil's wit, while Basil is shown saying there is never a time for laughter. Without a sentence joining them it reads as the quiz contradicting itself. With one, it is the best moment of her result.

Her real argument with Basil would be about hell (she hopes all are saved; Basil says eternal punishment has no end) and about reading the Bible for deeper meanings. The laugh line is the fun one, but one of the three lines should be the argument she would actually have.

The three lines are the generic ones (learning, anger, wealth), and P15 and P18 see some of the same Augustine lines. What really makes Daniel Augustine's man is war (Letter to Boniface), grace ('Give what You command, and command what You will') and seeking truth instead of leaving questions alone. Those lines would make a converted litigator say 'that's me'.
The On Christian Doctrine line ends mid-clause ('from those who have unlawful …'). The memorable part, the gold of the Egyptians, comes after the cut.

Antony's words come from Athanasius's Life of Antony, and the source is written three different ways on one card ('Athanasius, Life of Antony'; 'Life of Antony, by Athanasius'; 'Life of Antony, by Athanasius of Alexandria'). A precise reader will notice. Say it one way, for example 'as Athanasius remembered him'.
Antony's effort line ('virtue has need at our hands of willingness alone') is true to the Life, but a precise Catholic reader could take it for Pelagianism. A short plain lead-in would help.

Nyssa's body line opens with a clause no one can parse: 'The inefficiency of the body from either cause will be that which it guards against'. Start at 'train the flesh, neither making it wild … by excessive pampering, nor sickly … by immoderate mortification'.

Her most distinctive match, the hope that everyone returns to God, shows up only in the hook. Nyssa's own line on it is cut off ('to their primal …'). Trimmed to a whole sentence, it is the line she would screenshot.
Basil's church line is cut off at 'involves the …'.

Nyssa and Basil were brothers, and Nyssa's hook already says Basil called him too simple to be trusted. The reveal should say it outright: the one who would argue with you is your kindred spirit's big brother.

Hidden full-strength clash. He strongly agreed that it is right to weep openly (he lost a cousin in the 2017 Palm Sunday bombing), and Tertullian's recorded position is the strongest no: 'why should you grieve … That which you think to be death is departure'. The reveal shows only agreements, so his kindred spirit quietly holds the view that would hurt him most.

Tertullian won by a hair (0.57, against Benedict at 0.56 and Gregory the Great at 0.54). He was never counted a saint and ended outside the great Church. A Coptic deacon who reads the Desert Fathers in Arabic will know that and feel let down. The hook is charming, but it does not say this, and he will notice.
Tertullian's hell line is archaic ('directly ministers to their incorruptibility').

The sparring partner rests on five shared statements, and Nyssa agrees with him on three of them (weeping, anger, mystery). Nearly the whole distance comes from one statement, whether everyone will be saved. A sparring partner who agrees more than he disagrees does not feel like the farthest.
Nyssa is a saint he venerates. Only two lines show, and one is cut off ('to their primal …').

He could not answer the body or effort statements, because his Church holds both halves together (disciplining the body, and working with grace). The fasting at the centre of his life never reaches the result.
people.better: Benedict of Nursia, a hair behind (0.56). He agrees with him on saying less, on telling a brother his fault, on church discipline and on hell, with no full-strength clash, and a man who keeps two hundred fast days under a rule would see himself in Benedict's Rule. A tie-break that passes over a kindred spirit with a full-strength clash on a full-strength answer would pick him.

problems: Augustine agrees with him on all sixteen statements they share. That says more about Augustine having a position on nearly everything than it says about Jayden. Augustine is the kindred spirit of three of these ten (P12, P15, P18), and their lines overlap.

The lines are grown-up for a sixteen-year-old ('pious soul', 'covetousness', 'seasoned with an honest cheerfulness'). A more personal Augustine line for a loud drummer goes unused: 'I began to be more grieved at having refrained from saying what I ought to have said'.

None of the 22 statements touches what defines him (tongues at camp, prophecy, the Spirit's gifts today), so the result cannot see the Pentecostal in him. The early Church argued exactly this: Irenaeus heard believers 'speak all kinds of languages', Tertullian joined the New Prophecy, and Chrysostom and Augustine said those signs had passed.
Isaac's hook ('love for … even demons') may startle a Pentecostal teen, but in a good way. Keep it.

Isaac's nature line ends 'Written teachings have been added only after aberration'. A Lutheran who reads the catechism plainly may stop there and bristle. Cut it to the first sentence, the part he agreed with.

Isaac is a mountain hermit who warns against laughter, and Dale's dry joke is the best thing about him (he strongly agreed about a good laugh). The fit on silence and the land is real, but one line on the clash would keep it honest.

Lactantius is not someone a quiet Minnesota farmer would argue with. The only live clash is war. Two of the three lines do not show what they claim. The nature line is about philosophers failing at ethics, not about learning God from nature (and Lactantius argued from the design of the human body to God in On the Workmanship of God). The mystery line is 46 words, cut off mid-clause.
Isaac and Lactantius are also P17's exact pair, and two of the kindred lines are identical.
The source for Isaac's line on not correcting others is a treatise title over 30 words long. Cite 'Mystic Treatises' or 'Ascetical Homilies' and stop.
'Do not vituperate any one' and 'thee/thy' make a hard first read. A modern translation would land better.

Her best line is missing. She hopes all will be saved (with Julian of Norwich), and Isaac's line on it ('He repays them with resurrection instead of with justice') is the one she would copy into her journal.
Lactantius's calm line begins mid-sentence ('while they desire to free the soul …'). His wealth line is convoluted and does not clearly oppose her answer.

Unfair coding feeds this match. Lactantius is scored +1 on governments promoting the faith because of a dedication praising Constantine. His own famous position (Divine Institutes, book 5) is that religion cannot be forced and is defended by dying, not by killing. He also shares her pacifism, so the real distance between them is smaller than shown.

Augustine's body line reads as the opposite of the statement: 'they strive by a kind of toilsome exercise of the body itself to root out those lusts'. The same passage (On Christian Doctrine, book 1) says no one hates his own flesh. Use that sentence.

Hidden clash on his hottest topic. Augustine's recorded position is that the surplus of the rich belongs to the poor ('Thou possessest what belongs to others'), and that is the statement Andre called political. Showing only 'covetousness is condemned, not gold' flatters him. If he later finds the other line, he may feel sold.
Isaac's body line is a gift for an HVAC owner ('The knowledge of God does not dwell in a body that loves comfort'). Put it first.

An idea, not a confident swap: Clement of Alexandria wrote the early Church's one treatise defending wealth rightly used ('Who is the rich man that shall be saved?'), and he agrees with Andre on wealth, learning and the body. The data puts him seventh.
Hilary won on only five shared statements, and two of them are clashes (learning, nature). He has a position on only seven statements in all, so a player can land on him by coincidence.

The three lines suit her temper: a lie told to a killer, apostles with no state backing, 'the time for keeping silent is now past'. But her core is missing: voluntary poverty, the surplus belonging to the poor, nonviolence. Hilary is known for his doctrinal war with the Arians, not for any of those.
Hilary's lie line is cut off ('or …').

Gregory the Great is shown as her farthest, yet he holds her signature belief almost word for word: 'we do not bestow our own, but render them what is theirs; we rather pay a debt of justice' (Pastoral Rule). That is the Catholic Worker creed, and the reveal hides it. A 'where you'd agree' line would be fair to Gregory and would be the most delightful moment of her result.

Gregory's learning line is a fragment with no referent ('This thing we took so much amiss …'). It rebukes a bishop for teaching pagan poetry. It is not a stance on learning wisdom from non-Christians, and scoring it -2 overstates him.

With Lactantius's rulers position corrected to his own 'religion cannot be forced', he becomes her second (a Christian may never kill, not even in war; anger at wrong is right; against the Stoic calm). Not enough to unseat Hilary, but worth seeing.

The calling line reads badly out of context: 'those we suffer as adversaries on the way of God we should refuse to know, by hating and fleeing them'. It is Gregory's comment on Luke 14:26. Without the verse it looks like a pope telling people to hate their families, and it could end up on a share card.

The anger line is archaic and sounds violent ('Phinees … by his sword', 'quickened against himself the stirrings of the vengeance'). Use 'Phinehas' and a plainer sentence, or show the war or hell line, which matched him more strongly anyway.
Hidden full-strength clash on the statement he found most loaded (the extra belongs to the poor): Gregory calls giving to the poor paying them a debt of justice.

A pope as the kindred spirit may surprise a Baptist deacon. It is honest, and the hook (carried to St Peter's against his will) makes Gregory likeable. Augustine is second but far behind (0.66 vs 1.09). He would have been the easy 'that's me' for a man who teaches Romans.
Origen's war line opens 'none fight better for the king than we do', which reads as agreeing with Wayne until the twist. It works if he reads to the end.

works: The hooks are the best part: short, human and often funny (Augustine's pears, Nyssa's forged letters, Origen's mother hiding his clothes, Hilary sent home as 'a troubler of the East', Gregory carried to St Peter's). They make a stranger likeable before a single line is read.
The three-part line (the statement, your answer, his own words) shows exactly why, with no score. It reads as evidence, not a verdict.

Sparring partners work best when they are a vivid opposite in temperament with a short, plain line: Isaac against a loud teen drummer ('Be not friends with one that loves laughter'), Isaac against an HVAC owner ('The knowledge of God does not dwell in a body that loves comfort'), Origen against a literalist deacon, Basil against a choir alto who is quick to laugh, and Antony's fish line against a lawyer who reads theology on the train.

The kindred matches that land are strong: Augustine for the convert litigator, Isaac for the librarian who goes on silent retreats, Nyssa for the yoga teacher, Isaac for the farmer who says little, Nazianzen for the retiring alto.

Short, plain, complete quotes carry the reveal: Augustine's 'covetousness … not gold', Hilary on lying to a killer to protect someone in hiding, Tertullian on dreams, Isaac's 'Love silence above all things', Nyssa on sobs and tears.
Real families and friendships turn up without being planned (Nazianzen and Basil were best friends, Nyssa and Basil were brothers). That is a gift if the reveal names it.
change: Choose the lines by the centred score that made the match, not by raw answer times position. Raw picks the answers almost everyone gives (a good laugh, wealth used well), so three people see the same Augustine lines. Centred picks would give Daniel Augustine on war and 'Give what You command', Jayden Augustine regretting a silence, Ruth Isaac on resurrection instead of justice, and Wayne Gregory on war and hell. Keep at most one 'fun' line (laughter) per sparring partner.

Add one honest counter-line on each side. For the kindred spirit, add 'where he'd push back' when there is a full-strength clash (Tertullian on weeping for Mina, Gregory on the poor's due for Wayne, Augustine on surplus for Andre). For the sparring partner, add 'where you'd agree' (Gregory the Great with the Catholic Worker on the poor). It is fairer to the early Christian, it stops the player feeling misled when they find the other line later, and it is often the most delightful line on the card.

Guard against thin matches. MIN_SHARED 5 let Nazianzen (P11) and Hilary (P19) win on five statements, and made Nyssa P14's farthest on five statements where he agreed on three. Require about seven shared statements. Require clashes to outnumber agreements for a sparring partner. Break near-ties (under 0.05) against a kindred spirit with a full-strength clash on a full-strength answer (that picks Benedict for P14).

Hand-pick a display excerpt for every position: one or two complete sentences, under about 30 words, never starting mid-sentence ('while they desire …') and never ending on '…' mid-clause. Then check that the excerpt itself shows the position. Today Nazianzen on learning is cut before his point, Basil on church discipline before his, Nyssa's body line opens with an unreadable clause, Augustine's body line reads as fighting the body, Lactantius on nature is about ethics, and Gregory's learning line has no referent.

Modernise or re-source archaic translations for display (thee and thy, 'dischargest', 'vituperate', 'ministers to their incorruptibility', Phinees for Phinehas). Keep capitals for every pronoun for God.

Recheck three positions for fairness. Lactantius on rulers: the +1 comes from a dedication praising Constantine, but his signature position (Divine Institutes, book 5) is that religion cannot be forced, so it should be negative. This also changes P16 and P17's sparring partner. Lactantius on nature: -1 is doubtful for the author of On the Workmanship of God. Gregory the Great on learning: -2, from a rebuke of a bishop teaching pagan poetry, overstates him; -1 with that context is fairer.

Give the harsh lines the context they need, or pick others. Gregory's 'hating and fleeing' relatives is his comment on Luke 14:26, so say so. Nothing should reach a share card that makes a saint look cruel without his reason.

Name the relationship when the kindred spirit and the sparring partner knew each other: 'your kindred spirit's best friend' (Nazianzen and Basil), 'his big brother' (Nyssa and Basil), Jerome's quarrel by letter with Augustine. One sentence turns the reveal into a story.

Say plainly in the hook where Tertullian and Origen stand: Tertullian later joined the New Prophecy and is not counted a saint, and parts of Origen's teaching were condemned centuries after him. A devout player matched to either should not discover it later and feel the quiz hid it.

Tidy the details. Use one short date form ('c. 155 to after 220'; '7th century' instead of 'c. 613 to c. 700 (7th century)'). Use short work titles only (drop the 30-word treatise subtitle on Isaac). Remove the stray space before commas ('On the Judgment of God , his preface'). Credit words recorded by someone else one consistent way ('Antony, as Athanasius remembered him').

Add a statement on the Spirit's gifts today, for example 'God still gives gifts like prophecy and speaking in tongues'. The early Church split on it, with real lines on both sides (Irenaeus heard believers speaking in all kinds of languages; Tertullian's New Prophecy; Chrysostom and Augustine said those signs had passed), and it would let a Pentecostal player see himself. Also consider a statement on fasting, which is the centre of Coptic and Orthodox life and has strong lines on both sides, in place of the body statement, which splits what they hold together.

Watch Augustine as the default. He has a position on 20 of the 22 statements and took three of these ten (16 of 16 agreements for a Pentecostal teen). That is fine when the lines are personal and tiresome when three people get the same three.
